entry.title: Why brands are hungry for Min KyungJin
entry.summary: Creative Process Why brands are hungry for Min KyungJin The South Korean artist, also known as Sibatable, has built a practice around transforming food into unexpected objects. She talks to CR about bringing her distinctive approach to commercial work By Rebecca Fulleylove 20/11/
entry.content:
Creative Process

Why brands are hungry for Min KyungJin

The South Korean artist, also known as Sibatable, has built a practice around transforming food into unexpected objects. She talks to CR about bringing her distinctive approach to commercial work

By Rebecca Fulleylove 20/11/2026 7:20 am

“Food is hard to control. But if I control it too much, it starts to feel like a craft. Whatever I’m trying to express, I need it to still feel like food,” says culinary artist Min Kyungjin. “So I try to find a way through cooking, but sometimes I hit a dead end. When that happens, I write it down and pass it on to my future self.” Sometimes, with a little more experience, she figures it out.

Working under the moniker Sibatable, Kyungjin’s food creations have lit up the internet since she began sharing them in 2022. Having studied culinary arts at university, the South Korea-based creative was looking for an outlet. “Rather than showing myself, I expressed the things I loved through food and posted them on Instagram,” she says.  “The materials were all right there in my fridge.  Sharing those creations and connecting with people gradually grew into the work I do today.”

At first, she simply made things she liked – dogs, cats, rice koalas lying under an egg blanket. But the practice has since become even more playful, moving towards inanimate objects and everyday items like handbags, perfume bottles and socks, though the cute animals still make a welcome appearance.

entry.title: Andstudio creates maritime-inspired identity for Rotterdam bistro
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Andstudio creates maritime-inspired identity for Rotterdam bistro Werf’s rebrand aims to marry the location’s industrial past with contemporary urban life By Charlotte Rawlings 20/11/2026 3:03 am Vilnius-based creative agency andstudio has created a visual id
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Andstudio creates maritime-inspired identity for Rotterdam bistro

Werf’s rebrand aims to marry the location’s industrial past with contemporary urban life

By Charlotte Rawlings 20/11/2026 3:03 am

Vilnius-based creative agency andstudio has created a visual identity for Werf, a bar and bistro in Rotterdam, inspired by the destination’s industrial heritage and maritime setting.

Following its launch in autumn 2025, Werf’s revamped branding is part of a bid to bring the docklands closer to contemporary Rotterdam.

Based in Stadsdriehoek, the bistro is located beside a steep working slipway of the Koningspoort in the Oude Haven, where ships are still lowered into the harbour.

The 20-degree slope has informed the visual identity, with the logo, written in bold typography, also following this sharp angle. The inspiration does not stop at the ramps and slipways of Rotterdam, as the slanted text also pays homage to the raising of a glass or the tilt of a champagne bottle during fermentation.

Augustinas Paukštė, co-founder and creative director at andstudio, who led the redesign, said they didn’t want to “overcomplicate” the identity, describing Werf as “an honest, simple place”.

“We built the whole identity on one thing: the 20-degree angle of the Koningspoort slipway, where historic ships come out of the water to be restored.”

Seasonal colour palettes also pay homage to the ships docked at the wharf. The colour scheme of the menu is dictated by whichever ship is docked at the shipyard at the time.

The location gave the bistro its tagline, ‘Alles op de helling’, which translates literally to ‘everything on the slipway’, and figuratively ‘nothing is fixed’.

According to Paukštė, most of the inspiration came from the location itself, such as “the sharp steel structure of the cranes, the dock, and the mechanics of how a ship is pulled onto the slipway and launched back into the water”.

The andstudio team also read books on maritime history and shipbuilding to bring a piece of the working harbour into the bistro. “The hardest part was trusting that one single idea could carry the whole identity. It takes courage not to add more,” said Paukštė.

He also noted that his favourite part of the identity is the door stop, which can be found throughout the restaurant and the kitchen, leveraging the same 20-degree angle with the logo filling the space. “It also doubles as a wedge to level uneven table legs. It is a small detail, but it shows how far simplicity can go.”

He added that Werf’s personality comes through in “roughness and simplicity”. “That is not only the character of the bistro but of maritime culture as a whole: a bit rough around the edges, simple, made for everyone, and very romantic.”

entry.title: Wedge studio on how everything can be special
entry.summary: Creative Leadership Wedge studio on how everything can be special As Montreal and LA-based design studio Wedge reaches its 10th anniversary, it’s more determined, more optimistic, and more punk rock than ever By Emma Tucker 19/11/2026 3:29 am The first thing you see when you land
entry.content:
Creative Leadership

Wedge studio on how everything can be special

As Montreal and LA-based design studio Wedge reaches its 10th anniversary, it’s more determined, more optimistic, and more punk rock than ever

By Emma Tucker 19/11/2026 3:29 am

The first thing you see when you land on Wedge’s website is a simple sentence, emblazoned across the top: Everything Can Be Special. It’s a hopeful statement that feels absolutely right for the work the Montreal and LA design studio makes: clever, craft-steeped, soulful design that tunes into just the right level of nostalgia.

Wedge knows exactly what compels someone to pick up a brand. And they make it look effortless. “We really love what we do,” says co-founder and creative director Sarah Di Domenico. “We’re people who are excited by life, and I think that’s felt in the work. Joy is very important to us; I think it’s a very punk rock decision to choose joy.”

Di Domenico has been involved with the studio almost from the beginning, joining a year after design director Justin Lortie started it in 2016. “They were doing the most incredible work,” she says. “And I was looking through their decks and was like, well, you’re missing the story. That was my part.”

Di Domenico’s background is in the ad industry, creating campaigns for brands including Visa, HBO, Topshop and The North Face – doing the kind of truth-searching, storytelling work that she says would probably now fall under the title of ‘creative strategist’.

entry.title: How should brands design spaces for men?
entry.summary: Creative Insight How should brands design spaces for men? A new report by Seen Studios explores the nuances of masculinity in the modern age. Here, creative strategist Gursharan Panesar explains why brands should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to reach them By Gursharan Panes
entry.content:
Creative Insight

How should brands design spaces for men?

A new report by Seen Studios explores the nuances of masculinity in the modern age. Here, creative strategist Gursharan Panesar explains why brands should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to reach them

By Gursharan Panesar 19/11/2026 3:16 am

Between the manosphere, the self-improvement industry and the rise of the ‘performative male’, masculinity has become something of a cultural fixation. Yet for all the attention it receives, the conversation often reduces contradictory experiences to neat narratives about what men are becoming.

That was the starting point for Peak Man, our recent research report at Seen Studios. Through moderated conversations between pairs of male friends across London, Paris, New York, Tokyo and Accra, we explored how they negotiate changing expectations around success, identity and progress.

Men have more ways to define themselves, but also an expanding list of things they feel they ought to improve. And increasingly, self-improvement isn’t something men pursue alone. It’s become a social activity, shaping where they gather, how they spend time together and their expectations.

entry.title: Welcome to Vice City: how brands hijacked the GTA VI launch
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Welcome to Vice City: how brands hijacked the GTA VI launch From epic city takeovers to sun-kissed social posts, we explore how brands have tapped into the world’s most hotly anticipated video game By Charlotte Rawlings 19/11/2026 1:04 am After 13 years, mult
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Welcome to Vice City: how brands hijacked the GTA VI launch

From epic city takeovers to sun-kissed social posts, we explore how brands have tapped into the world’s most hotly anticipated video game

By Charlotte Rawlings 19/11/2026 1:04 am

After 13 years, multiple delays and even more leaks, Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI is finally available to play.

Despite the action-adventure game continuing its tradition of zero product placement (this time within the satirical setting of Leonida, a fictional state inspired by Florida), brands have been falling over themselves to get in on the action. A surprising turn of events, perhaps, given that the series has earned itself a controversial reputation since its initial launch in 1997.

With its depictions of violence, sex and substance use, GTA is not typically something brands would want to touch with a 10-foot pole; unlike, say, the Barbie phenomenon of 2023. However, GTA VI has broken all the usual rules.

Is it because today’s marketers grew up playing GTA? Or are its themes simply no longer shocking in our current media landscape? Either way, a cultural moment this massive has proved too lucrative to ignore, particularly after titles like Epic Games’ Fortnite proved gaming’s commercial power. Below we round up some of the biggest brand moments attached to the game so far.

MEDIA, ENTERTAINMENT AND EDITORIAL

Netflix aired a preview of GTA VI gameplay in August. Fans were invited to watch the 27-minute film at a specific time (3pm ET) and had a six-hour window of exclusivity before it was shared widely on Rockstar Games’ YouTube channel and the official GTA VI website. This restricted viewing window turned the preview into an event for fans, fuelling conversation around a specific moment.

Animated sitcom South Park also featured 20 seconds of gameplay in one of its episodes in October. True to the show’s toilet-style humour, the footage shows a dog doing its business on a beach before Jason, one of the main characters in the game, picks up the poo and attacks the NPC dog walker with it.

Jason and fellow protagonist Lucia were also treated like A-list stars when they appeared on the covers of magazines such as Dazed, Love and Edge.

OUTDOOR AND CITY TAKEOVERS

Rockstar took worldbuilding to the extreme when it transformed Miami into Vice City. Neon colours flooded the city with special builds, while supercars took to the streets to immerse locals and visitors. A ‘Welcome to Vice City’ sign also appeared on the Kaseya Center roof, while digital billboards advertised fictional GTA brands such as Pfister and Weazel News.

The transformation was captured by creators and posted on social media. One creator also followed the Goodyear Blimp as it took to the skies sporting the magenta Vice City logo. The blimp travelled from Ohio through North Carolina down to south Florida.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Nick 🎬 | Miami Videographer (@shotbygallo)

Rockstar and West Coast Customs brought some of GTA’s cars to the real world, including the Grotti Cheetah, Pegassi Tempesta and Progen Emerus. The cars were driven around Miami and filmed for social media.

This later resulted in hyper-realistic street clips, featuring the same cars, being posted on Only in Dade, a network focused on Miami-Dade County, or Vice-Dale County in the game. This footage appeared to look a lot like gameplay and had fans speculating if Rockstar had shared another teaser of the game. Suspicions were raised further when Rockstar liked and reposted the video.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by ONLY in DADE (@onlyindade)

Giant outdoor ads promoting the game showed up in major cities including Paris, New York and Tokyo. GTA VI-inspired murals also appeared on Miami’s Wynwood Walls, the city’s outdoor street art museum, with Miami-Dade County locals receiving free admission. Wynwood Walls teamed up with the game to create the Wynwood Walls Art of Vice City merchandise collection.

LIVE EXPERIENCES

As part of the city takeover, E11even Miami assumed the form of GTA VI’s nightclub, Nine1nine. The month-long takeover, running from November 6 to December 6, included an appearance from musician Flo Rida at the grand opening. A GTA VI launch party will also take place on November 20.

Meanwhile, shoppers in the London can visit Vice City at Selfridges’ The Corner Shop as the game takes over the pop-up space from November 9-28. A custom Grotti Cheetah takes centre stage and is available to purchase for £1 million via Selfridges Personal Shopping.

Elsewhere, on November 18, basketball team Miami Heat marked the launch with record label Cactus Jack. Kaseya Center, home to the Miami Heat, featured custom Vice City courts, collaborative Nike x Travis Scott uniforms/Air Force Ones, and pop-up concessions for GTA’s fictional fast-food chains Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell.

UNOFFICIAL COLLABS

Naturally, there are many brands that haven’t secured an official partnership with GTA VI – but that hasn’t stopped them from joining in on the fun. Xbox, for example, is rather limited with the promotion it can do around the release, due to PlayStation having an exclusive marketing deal with Rockstar.

So it commissioned an unusual custom-made gaming console, which sits inside the stomach of an alligator, presumably taking inspiration from the games’ ties to Florida. Fans had the chance to win the ‘X-Bite’ console in a competition, which was at the centre of a global social campaign.

KFC Australia is hosting a mock funeral on launch day to give those who weren’t forward-thinking enough to book the day off the perfect excuse. People could bid farewell to the fictional deceased, named ‘Ann Alibi’, during working hours on November 19 at KFC Robina, Queensland, or via a livestream.

In the UK, the NHS unexpectedly got involved when its social media admin posted that they were recovering from surgery on their hand. The post included pictures of their hand in a thick bandage accompanied by the caption ‘NHS England social media manager in race to be fit for release of GTA6’. The post also took the opportunity to educate scrollers and gamers alike on the dangers of repetitive strain injury.

Mondelēz’s Southeast Asian cookie brand ChipsMore leant into the game’s 18+ age restriction via QR-coded Discord tutorials for locked-out younger siblings. These excluded gamers can instead learn tips and tricks for Malaysia’s most popular competitive games.

STEALTHY SOCIAL TIE-INS

Finally, a wave of brands piggybacked on the launch through some low-risk social media posts that placed them inside the game without infringing on its IP. Car manufacturers such as Mini, BMW and Hyundai posted images of their vehicles in neon-coloured, sun-soaked settings. KitKat France, Burger King New Zealand and Deutsche Telekom also plunged into the world of Vice City with posts cheekily nodding to the big day.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by MINI (@mini)

If the above is anything to go by, it’s clear why there is no need for GTA VI to court brand partnerships; it has built a world so iconic that companies are lining up to promote it for free. Genuine brands may still be absent from the streets of Leonida, but out in the real world, Vice City is officially open for business.

entry.title: Mttr and Studio Sutherl& go analogue with Ctlg
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Mttr and Studio Sutherl& go analogue with Ctlg Co-founded by Bob Shankly and Studio Sutherl&’s Jim Sutherland, the zero-waste denim brand is swapping Instagram algorithms for offline conversations through a seasonally printed catalogue By Rebecca Fulleylove 1
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Mttr and Studio Sutherl& go analogue with Ctlg

Co-founded by Bob Shankly and Studio Sutherl&’s Jim Sutherland, the zero-waste denim brand is swapping Instagram algorithms for offline conversations through a seasonally printed catalogue

By Rebecca Fulleylove 18/11/2026 8:30 am

In an age when brands are pressured to feed social media algorithms and reduce interactions to clicks, Mttr is taking an alternative route through a seasonally printed catalogue.

Co-founded by Bob Shankly and Studio Sutherl& founder Jim Sutherland, Mttr produces a single circular, zero-waste pair of jeans made from discarded materials. Rather than churning out seasonal fashion collections, the brand keeps its garment fixed while letting its ideas evolve through Ctlg (short for catalogue), a tactile publication that questions the value of the digital marketing machine that has become the default for most businesses.

For Shankly and Sutherland, the decision wasn’t just about what they wanted to say, but how they said it. Social media might have offered a cheaper route to an audience, but the mechanics of modern content creation didn’t feel appealing. “The thought of us holding little mics to our faces and saying ‘hey guys’ sends us cold,” they admit.

“We’re not ‘anti-social’, it’s just the idea of endlessly feeding the Insta machine doesn’t appeal to us,” they explain. “The audience are not really Mttr’s followers, they are Meta’s users, and Meta can put them out of reach at the touch of a button.”

Instead, they favour a slower, offline conversation – an approach that has already yielded unexpected results. Following the launch of Ctlg for instance, the pair were invited by Sir Paul Smith to his Covent Garden office to talk denim, later returning to spend a day looking through his books while he was away. “To us, that’s real ‘engagement’,” they say.

The publication also sidesteps the visual shorthand usually associated with sustainability. Rather than adopting muted colours or an overtly ecological aesthetic, Studio Sutherl& wanted an identity that felt connected to the denim industry.

“We wanted the typography and identity to be timeless, with a nod to the industry Mttr works in,” they explain. “The classic, cut letterforms of Dala Moa by Paul Barnes do that beautifully, combined with the more utilitarian Söhne.” The result feels closer to an independent cultural journal than a conventional corporate brochure.

Physicality is central to that character. Hand-stitched cyanotypes and exposed thread interact directly with Jim Marsden’s photography, encouraging readers to handle the object rather than scan it. For Sutherland, this reflects a wider creative response to the encroachment of AI.

“As AI invades every aspect of our lives (even though we never asked for it), I feel the creative push back – or perhaps opportunity – will be a period of ‘extreme analogue’,” he says. “The Mttr Ctlg, I think, is a step in that direction.”

That ethos extends to its editorial structure, which takes its cue from the four values behind the Mttr acronym (Make noise. Not jeans. / Think ‘forever’. / Truth be told. / Respect. Reject.).

Each seasonal edition is divided into four parts: a nature-led photographic shoot; an artist responding to the question ‘What Matters?’; a section called ‘Thinking Allowed’, featuring four creative voices; and Studio Sutherl&’s playful exploration of the more-than-human world. Contributors so far include Nina and Jack of Studiomama, Daniel Freytag, Sophie Sellu, Sarah Boris, writers Nick Parker, Mark Shayler and Rob Lowe (Supermundane), and data artist Rebecca Kaye.

Rather than chasing metrics, Mttr is working to a more peaceful brief. “We’re not hoping for a ‘viral moment’ with the Ctlg,” they say. “‘Sitting quietly’ is just fine with us.”

Ultimately, the pair view Mttr as a publishing company more than a denim label, aiming to produce a publication worthy of mag shop shelves. Alongside future seasonal editions, they are planning to compile the first four issues into a single expanded volume, provisionally titled Once Around The Sun.

For a label built around a single zero-waste garment, an intricate print catalogue might seem an unlikely place to invest resources. Yet that contradiction is kind of the point. As Shankly and Sutherland put it: “If you’re making something the world doesn’t need, you better be sure you’re making a difference.”

entry.title: How Lola Madrid turns crazy ambition into serious work
entry.summary: Creative Insight How Lola Madrid turns crazy ambition into serious work The Spanish agency has released a steady stream of striking work this year for the likes of De’Longhi and Magnum, proving that their mantra is working By Adam Woodward 18/11/2026 3:44 am Under executive creat
entry.content:
Creative Insight

How Lola Madrid turns crazy ambition into serious work

The Spanish agency has released a steady stream of striking work this year for the likes of De’Longhi and Magnum, proving that their mantra is working

By Adam Woodward 18/11/2026 3:44 am

Under executive creative director Tomás Ostiglia, Lola Madrid has built a reputation for producing work that can look slick one minute and strange, even slightly unruly, the next – but always rooted in a clear point of view.

Lola’s approach has been distilled into a recently unveiled positioning: ‘Crazy ambition makes serious things happen.’ This sounds like a contradiction: how can you be ‘crazy’ and ‘serious’ at the same time? “I think most of the time, you’re not always 100% sure about what you’re doing,” Ostiglia elaborates. “We’re crazy ambitious, but we have the conviction to make really serious things happen. You follow the idea. That’s how we work.”

That thinking is increasingly evident in Lola’s work for brands including Magnum, Axe/Lynx and De’Longhi, while the agency itself now reaches far beyond its home in the Spanish capital. Originally conceived within the MullenLowe network by Fernando Vega Olmos in 2007 as a boutique, pan-European agency, with Unilever as its founding client, Lola has since become a global operation with hubs in New York, Los Angeles and São Paulo, all sitting within TBWA Worldwide. Yet Madrid remains its gravitational centre.

Ostiglia, who joined the company in 2014 before being appointed ECD five years later, describes steering the agency through this exciting period of expansion as one of the most challenging experiences of his career. “It’s a lot of work because we’re trying to secure the culture. We’re based in Madrid, but we have people from all over the world. I’m from Argentina, and we have this history of bringing really good creative talent from Latin America to Europe [the name Lola was derived from Lowe Latina]. That’s still an important part of our DNA.”

For CEO Tom Elliston, the agency’s international mix is reflected in its unusual structure, which is weighted much more towards the creative side than any other department. Of its 74 permanent staff at the last count, around two-thirds are creatives. “If you look at the split in other agencies, it would be a lot heavier on account management, planning and so on. What I’m trying to say is that we put everything into the product of our work.”

We’re crazy ambitious, but we have the conviction to make really serious things happen. You follow the idea. That’s how we work

Ostiglia adds that while he and Elliston might be viewed as traditional because of their age, the wider creative team is “full of young people doing so much cool shit”. “They’re not as rooted in traditional advertising. There’s a lot more social and digital work now, but again, it’s all about the way we work,” he says. “A really solid story, with an amazing concept and a super-solid brand strategy, will always work,” he says. “Then you can play around with it to create a bigger universe to connect with the audience.”

Take Axe/Lynx’s Power of a Fragrance platform, which has generated everything from traditional campaign films to more unexpected executions, including an interactive scratch-and-sniff billboard campaign and more tongue-in-cheek, product-led ideas such as a luxury perfume bottle holder for the brand’s body spray cans.

Then there’s De’Longhi. When the agency first started working with the Italian coffee-machine brand in 2025, they might have been expected to stick to the category’s tried-and-trusted celebrity route: Brad Pitt was already attached to the business – and you don’t say no to Brad Pitt. But a trip to the factory changed Lola’s understanding of what it was actually selling. “We saw the ads and it was the usual bean-to-coffee story. That was what they’d been saying: here’s Brad Pitt having a coffee,” Ostiglia explains. “Suddenly they brought the designers of the machines into the meeting.

They started telling us about the Italian design and showing us the machines. We said, ‘What the fuck, why is this not in the communication? You’re not selling coffee. You’re machine designers. You design the Ferraris of coffee.’”

Bye bye, Brad? Not quite – he remains a valuable asset, fronting the latest chapter of De’Longhi’s Perfetto campaign via a spot directed by Spike Jonze that was released in September (following last year’s effort from Taika Waititi). More conventional, premium advertising has not gone out the window entirely then. But 2026 has seen a crucial development for the brand: the machine itself is now the hero.

For Elliston, campaigns such as Perfetto and The World’s Smallest Coffee Shop, which transformed De’Longhi’s machines into miniature coffee shops, show what happens when an agency looks beyond the fixed boundaries of a client brief. “It’s very easy to focus on all the politics of what you can’t do,” he says. “But once you take time to really understand the brand, the ambition, the ideas, everything flows from that.”

In the case of Perfetto, he continues, “we were told, Brad Pitt won’t talk to camera, he won’t do jokes, he won’t do this or that”. “But we knew the strength of our idea and what we wanted to say, so we just kept pushing. Eventually Brad Pitt himself looked at it and said, ‘Yeah, I like it. It’s a good idea. I’ll do it.’ We’re proud of the work, but also, in terms of our client relationships, we’ve got some very strong, long-standing relationships.

“To be honest, we haven’t got many clients, but they’ve all come from a referral of someone who’s worked with us before, which is a good sign of confidence. We’ve been inherent in building these brands with them. The great challenge with a brand like Magnum or Axe/Lynx is, can you define the positioning of the brand with just one word? That’s where our best brand building lives.”

Lola’s recent work for Magnum has continued to build on a creative territory that the agency has been gradually refining for nearly two decades. In Nothing Cracks Like Magnum, the brand’s famous chocolate crack acts as the central visual device, turning a simple product characteristic into a recognisable signifier of its single-word proposition: ‘pleasure’.

We don’t want to do shocking ideas for the sake of it. We’re crazy because that’s the way to build a brand. You can’t just throw fireworks in any direction

This is what Ostiglia means when he talks about being ‘crazy’ with a purpose. It’s not about creating work that puts visibility above effectiveness, or novelty above longevity. “We don’t want to do shocking ideas for the sake of it,” he says. “We’re crazy because that’s the way to build a brand. If you do things just to stand out, well, so what? We stretch our ideas to build the brands we work with. You can’t just throw fireworks in any direction. Each idea and each campaign is part of a bigger strategy.”

Aside from building brands, Ostiglia and Elliston are currently focused on Lola’s own growth. The agency’s micro-network is now part of the expanded Omnicom group following its acquisition of IPG last year, but Madrid has retained a degree of independence that allows it to operate more like a creative studio. The aim, then, is to maintain its high standards as it expands. As Ostiglia puts it: “Our dream is to keep hold of this beautiful thing and make it better, better, better, not just bigger.”

The most obvious recent expression of Lola Madrid’s operational freedom is its collaboration with Ostiglia’s design hero, David Carson, who was invited to “destroy” the agency’s work and “bring it together again” as a way of reinterpreting the agency’s new positioning. “What I love is you can feel the process,” Ostiglia says. “It’s 100% human.”

While much of Lola Madrid’s work champions human craft, like everyone else, the agency is experimenting with AI. Yet Ostiglia’s interest in the technology appears to lie less in its capabilities than in what its adoption has so far exposed: namely, the limits of automation when it comes to things like intuition, imperfection and the creative leaps required to make an idea feel genuinely new.

“The mystery of creativity, of our own beautiful human stupidity, is hard to replicate. I don’t have a clue what’s going to happen in the future, but my feeling is that mystery will somehow remain. What excites me is, what can we do that you don’t see coming? What’s the best way to get someone to think, ‘Fuck, where has this come from?’ There are people who are really smart, who can turn emotions into numbers. But the magic of creating something is profoundly imperfect. That’s my goal: to try to manipulate some of that magic.”

entry.title: Wunder Werkz gives Denver Design District a new identity
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Wunder Werkz gives Denver Design District a new identity The design studio has created a bold visual identity for the area as it expands beyond interior design professionals and fosters a retail, food and arts hub By Rebecca Fulleylove 18/11/2026 3:40 am Wund
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Wunder Werkz gives Denver Design District a new identity

The design studio has created a bold visual identity for the area as it expands beyond interior design professionals and fosters a retail, food and arts hub

By Rebecca Fulleylove 18/11/2026 3:40 am

Wunder Werkz has developed a new identity for Denver Design District, as the Colorado neighbourhood looks to broaden its appeal beyond the interior design trade.

Once primarily a destination for industry professionals, the area is now looking to attract a wider audience through a growing mix of design retail, art, food and other cultural offerings.

“The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, partner at Wunder Werkz.

“Trade remains an important part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”

The identity starts with a palette of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow, bringing brighter tones to an area otherwise characterised by the tans and greys of its built environment. Its central mark, formed from three progressively compressed Ds, takes a geometric approach. Designed to feel both solid and in motion, it provides a shorthand for the district’s name.

Wunder Werkz has also developed DDD Standard, a bespoke mid-weight sans serif used across the wordmark and wider identity. Loosely referencing the mid-century furniture forms of Herbert Bayer, the typeface balances architectural structure with more playful details.

Its numerals were given particular attention, with large-scale applications such as building identification and signage in mind. A set of silhouetted product icons completes the graphics, depicting different design categories and helping visitors find their way around.

Beyond just printed materials and digital branding, the identity has been carried onto the buildings themselves. Each has been given its own colour designation, repeated across external signage, directories and other navigational elements.

The approach is also visible in a new sculptural aluminium sign for Denver Design District, installed alongside Herbert Bayer’s Articulated Wall, which has stood in the area since the 1980s.

The website has undergone a similar rethink. Bringing together shop directories, maps, events and editorial content, it caters to both regular trade visitors looking for specific businesses and newcomers wanting to get a better sense of what the district has to offer.

entry.title: Jonathan Glazer directs uncanny short film for Gentle Monster
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Jonathan Glazer directs uncanny short film for Gentle Monster The cinematic ad campaign stars Joaquin Phoenix and offers a first look at Gentle Monster’s intelligent eyewear collection By Eliza Williams 17/11/2026 2:03 pm Reality and fantasy blur in Jonathan
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Jonathan Glazer directs uncanny short film for Gentle Monster

The cinematic ad campaign stars Joaquin Phoenix and offers a first look at Gentle Monster’s intelligent eyewear collection

By Eliza Williams 17/11/2026 2:03 pm

Reality and fantasy blur in Jonathan Glazer’s compelling new short film, which sees Joaquin Phoenix play a salesman who has a series of strange encounters in an impeccably designed hotel, which become increasingly dreamlike and bizarre.

Echoing both Stanley Kubrick’s classic film The Shining and recent A24 hit Backrooms, the film’s weird moments begin early on, when Phoenix experiences a deeply odd interaction at the check-in desk. He nonetheless takes this in his stride, and soon settles into his mid-century modern suite.

Yet when he is awoken from a nap by mysterious noises, he is compelled to investigate. The film then takes a turn for the surreal as time bends and Phoenix alights upon a pair of unexpected characters in the midst of a fight.

Phoenix once again shows remarkable composure in the face of the bizarre, and instead of immediately getting the hell out of there, he turns to his Gentle Monster glasses for assistance, using their in-built tech to translate and communicate with the creatures and make sense of the new world he has discovered.

The film certainly stands apart from the intelligent eyewear advertising we’ve been presented with from other brands, proving to be a product demo of the most surreal kind while retaining the deep fashion associations we have with Gentle Monster. Plus Glazer’s direction is witty, odd and beautiful, and – as ever – impossible to look away from.

entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Pentagram rebrands Greece’s Alpha Bank around legacy symbol

Based on an ancient Greek coin, the bank’s primary symbol forms the centrepiece of a striking new identity that blends heritage with contemporary design

By Daniel Milroy Maher 17/11/2026 3:25 am

Alpha Bank, one of Greece’s oldest and largest financial groups, has partnered with Pentagram on a new identity, inspired by its rich history. Established in 1879, the Athens-based bank has been a central figure in Greek society ever since its founding, sponsoring and preserving Greek culture and heritage for decades.

Now, amid a shifting financial landscape, and with desires to modernise the business, Alpha Bank felt it was time to refresh and future-proof its branding. The brief for the Pentagram team was to develop an identity that could maintain Alpha Bank’s competitive position within the market, while appealing to a broad demographic of young professionals and affluent older customers, as well as societal and institutional stakeholders.

Pentagram partner Domenic Lippa, who led the project, says that Alpha Bank was an ideal collaborator from the outset, and “was willing to explore different opportunities, and in doing so, push the brief further”. He continues: “Once that creative door was opened, we could go in different directions, but what I felt quite early was that the emotional strength of the legacy was the symbol.”

The symbol Lippa refers to is, of course, the Alpha Bank logo, which has remained the same since its founding nearly 150 years ago. It is based on an ancient Greek coin called a silver stater, one of which can be found in the Bank’s extensive numismatic collection. Emerging in the 8th century BC, the stater was the first coin to be used in the markets of the Mediterranean and the East, and served as an ideal muse for one of the country’s premier banks.

However, feeling that Alpha Bank’s stater symbol “had lost some of its quality” over time, Lippa and his team chose to gently rework the logo, separating the graphic element from the wordmark and redrawing it so that it appears thinner, elongated and more contemporary. Lippa explains: “The symbol needed to become the emotional heart for the brand. Like it was originally. For this to happen, we needed to liberate it from the wordmark. The wordmark itself needed to be less formal but still retain the authority for the bank.”

Where the wordmark is concerned, Pentagram chose to replace the old font with new custom typefaces, called Alpha Sans and Alpha Text. The former, developed in partnership with type designer Tom Baber, features five different weights and does much of the heavy lifting across the identity, while the latter serves as a functional typeface for use at smaller sizes.

Colour was also an important consideration for the design team, and offered yet another chance to champion Alpha Bank’s strong heritage. Revolving around the existing Alpha Blue, which has been at the heart of the bank’s identity for decades, Pentagram added new key colours such as white and Galazio Blue, as well as a secondary palette of Thalassi Turquoise, Heritage Pink and Alpha Gold. Five other brighter hues were also introduced to be used for digital elements such as infographics.

Along with the logo and colour palette, Pentagram developed a series of abstract and logo patterns inspired by aspects of the Alpha Bank symbol; a series of useful brand icons also based on the symbol; and a suite of striking brand imagery that captures real people and everyday moments to evoke feelings of trust and positivity.

Together, these elements make for an identity that is deeply rooted in Alpha Bank’s past, and at the same time heavily invested in its future. Cleaner, sharper and better equipped for the digital age, it also retains the bank’s reputation for warmth and dependability.

Reflecting on the project’s success, Lippa notes: “I believe within any project we are eternally searching for the truth in the solution. To discover the truth, you need a client willing to help you go on that journey. The team at Alpha Bank gave us 110% of their time, knowledge and ambition. Without them we would never have managed to find what we were searching for.”

entry.summary: Creative Leadership A look inside a great CMO-agency relationship When a brand CMO and its ad agency are attuned strategically and creatively, magic – and money – can follow. Here, we examine the results of the recent partnership between Telstra and agency Bear Meets Eagle On Fir
entry.content:
Creative Leadership

A look inside a great CMO-agency relationship

When a brand CMO and its ad agency are attuned strategically and creatively, magic – and money – can follow. Here, we examine the results of the recent partnership between Telstra and agency Bear Meets Eagle On Fire

By Eliza Williams 17/11/2026 3:10 am

In March this year, it was announced that Brent Smart, CMO at Australian telco Telstra since 2022, was stepping down. On the surface, this might seem like no big deal. After all, CMOs move on from brands with increasing haste these days. But Smart had brought huge change to Telstra and, in partnership with Micah Walker and the team at Sydney-based agency Bear Meets Eagle On Fire, is credited with reinvigorating the brand.

Reflecting on the Telstra he joined in 2022, Smart acknowledges that while the “business was in great shape”, the brand reputation wasn’t. “Telstra was a brand people didn’t like much,” he says. “Most of the budget was going into retail offers and performance marketing – any brand work was very corporate. They created a huge volume of work but it was pretty templated and forgettable. I had a clear narrative from the get-go that would guide all our work and link it back to the reputation challenge – if you want to change how people feel about the brand, you need to change how the brand feels.”

Smart and Walker had worked together before on projects for insurance company IAG, where Bear created work for the firm’s largest brand, NRMA, and also created a new digital insurance brand, Rollin’, from scratch. “When I joined Telstra, I wanted the same sort of thinking and level of craft that Bear always brings,” says Smart. “I see Micah as more of a partner than an agency creative leader. I welcome his push – there’s no one’s taste I trust more.”

entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

New book charts Tadanori Yokoo’s illustrious career

Edited by Mark Holborn, this detailed retrospective delves into the striking work and living legacy of the famed Japanese visual artist

By Daniel Milroy Maher 16/11/2026 10:07 am

Thames & Hudson has released the first comprehensive English-language retrospective of famed Japanese visual artist Tadanori Yokoo. The new publication spans Yokoo’s entire career, from his emergence in the 1960s in Tokyo to his ongoing work at the age of 90.

Born in Nishikawa in 1936, Yokoo’s first foray into the creative industry was as a commercial designer, which, while restrictive, gave him the technical foundation he needed to refine, and later to expand, his personal practice.

He soon moved to Tokyo, where his work drifted into the avant-garde, and his experimental approach to graphic design, illustration and painting earned him a reputation (especially among the city’s radical youth) as a groundbreaking visual artist. Over the years, this reputation grew, solidifying his place as one of Japan’s most celebrated cultural figures.

In this monograph, readers can explore his unique blend of original pre-psychedelic imagery, Pop Art, sexual iconography, and references to Japanese historical tradition, such as ukiyo-e prints. Presented chronologically, the featured work also traces Yokoo’s evolving focal points throughout his life, from post-war consumer culture in the 60s to spirituality and mysticism in the 70s, and then finally to memory and mortality from the 80s onwards.

The latter theme is particularly prominent in Yokoo’s story, with Holborn writing in the book’s introduction that “the beginning [of his story], in fact, lies not in the early graphic work, although that provides a visual introduction, but in memory…. As he gets older, his memory becomes increasingly pertinent. The resource of the subconscious, from which the work arises, becomes yet more pronounced, and so the events of the past determine what comes from Yokoo’s brush in his studio [today].”

Across the chapters of the book, readers are given similar insights into the interests, beliefs and sensibilities of Yokoo. There are many quotes from previous interviews he has given, in which he discusses his creative process, the themes of his work, and his world view more generally. His influence on, and collaborations with, other writers and artists are also explored – most notably his work with the renowned Japanese novelist and playwright Yukio Mishima.

Crucially, for Holborn, editing this book was about more than just documenting Yokoo’s fascinating and extensive oeuvre; it was also a long-term effort to “reinforce the narrative of his life”. As the author explains, “His work defines that narrative. Here, I am simply joining up the threads as they become evident in the course of the work.”

Tadanori Yokoo is published by Thames & Hudson; thamesandhudsonusa.com
